title: Bond Premiums & Discounts
description: Understand why bonds issue above or below face value and how carrying amount changes.
html:
Why don't bonds always sell at face value?

The stated interest rate on a bond may be different from the market interest rate investors currently demand.

Remember this relationship

  • Stated Rate = Market Rate → Face Value
  • Stated Rate < Market Rate → Discount
  • Stated Rate > Market Rate → Premium

Bond issued at a discount

Suppose a $100,000 bond pays 6% interest, but investors demand an 8% return.

The bond's contractual interest payments are less attractive than the market requires.

Therefore, investors will generally pay less than $100,000.

Stated Rate < Market Rate → Bond Discount

Bond issued at a premium

Now suppose the $100,000 bond pays 10%, while investors demand only 8%.

The bond's contractual interest payments are relatively attractive, so investors may pay more than $100,000.

Stated Rate > Market Rate → Bond Premium

Carrying amount

The carrying amount is the amount at which the bond liability is reported after considering an unamortized discount or premium.

Discount

Carrying Amount < Face Value

Premium

Carrying Amount > Face Value

What happens over time?

As the discount or premium is amortized, the bond's carrying amount moves toward its face value.

Discount Bond

Carrying amount increases toward face value.

Premium Bond

Carrying amount decreases toward face value.

CPA shortcut

Discount → carrying amount climbs.

Premium → carrying amount falls.

Both move toward face value.

quiz.prompt: A bond has a 6% stated rate when investors demand an 8% market rate. The bond will generally issue at:
quiz.explanation: Because the stated rate is below the market rate, investors generally pay less than face value, creating a bond discount.
